title: Ansel and the Inventory
premise: Elodie Dravenmoor returns to her late mother's crumbling house to prepare it for sale, armed with a ledger in which she records everything her mother never said—apologies withheld, names unspoken, a childhood of careful silence. Behind the wardrobe she finds a box of letters her mother wrote but never sent: to Elodie, to a sister erased from family memory, to a man whose name explains everything. Reading them forces Elodie to confront that her mother's invisibility was a survival strategy she inherited. At the estate sale, with buyers walking through the rooms, Elodie reads the final letter aloud to the empty house, says goodbye properly, and leaves the ledger on the hall table—choosing speech over silence as the door closes behind her.
about_author: Freya Vane is the pen name of a former estate appraiser who spent a decade cataloguing other people's inheritances before writing her own. She lives in a coastal town full of houses waiting to be emptied, and writes about the objects we keep and the words we don't.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Elodie, POV, arrives at the house three days after the funeral and begins her inventory: rooms, furniture, and a parallel ledger of everything her mother never said. The emotional beat is controlled grief—she catalogues to avoid feeling, and the reader sees how fluently she speaks in lists instead of words.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Elodie, POV. Clearing her mother's bedroom, she finds a box of forty-one unsent letters wedged behind the wardrobe. She reads the first three: one to herself at age nine, one to an Aunt Vera no one ever mentioned, one beginning 'My darling, I should have told you.' The beat is vertigo—the inventory was wrong; her mother said everything, just to no one.

chapters.title: What Vera Knew
chapters.summary: Elodie, POV, tracks down Vera, now ninety and sharp, in a care home two towns away. Vera reveals the family rupture—her sister chose silence to survive a marriage, and taught Elodie the same habit without meaning to. The emotional beat is rising anger and recognition: Elodie has been her mother's daughter all along, invisible by design.

chapters.title: Read Aloud, Before the Sale
chapters.summary: Climax and resolution. Elodie, POV, on the morning of the estate sale, reads the final letter—the one addressed simply 'To whoever is left'—out loud in the empty kitchen, her voice cracking on the apology her mother finally made. She leaves the ledger and the letters on the hall table for whoever comes next, and walks out speaking her goodbye to the street.
